Need To Know
Alaska's Sullivan Showdown
President Donald Trump
called for
Alaska Democratic Senate nominee Mary Peltola to be prosecuted and removed from the ballot after a
New York Times report
(free w/email) alleged her campaign recruited a candidate sharing the name of her opponent, Sen. Dan Sullivan (R).
Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy (R) also ordered an investigation Wednesday, days before Tuesday’s midterms. The effort reportedly began in 2025, and Peltola’s former campaign manager said she was aware of it but wasn’t directly involved. Peltola’s campaign denies involvement, as does the second Sullivan, a retired teacher who is one of four candidates in the race. State election officials initially disqualified him over concerns about voter confusion, but the Alaska Supreme Court reinstated his candidacy. The Justice Department
sued last week
to block certification of a Peltola victory if confusion over the second Sullivan affected the outcome.
In a Sullivan twist, Anchorage's former mayor—a third Dan Sullivan—endorsed the incumbent in August. Why are there
so many Dan Sullivans
in Alaska?

Chinese Spy Targets Nvidia
US intelligence agencies believe Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is the
target of a Chinese spy
, according to
a New York Times report
(free w/email).
Alice Huang, who is unrelated to the Nvidia CEO, is a senior executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, which has been accused of smuggling AI chips into China. The pair were seen together at a Taipei bar in 2024 and a restaurant in 2025, interactions Nvidia is defending as standard business engagement. President Donald Trump was reportedly briefed on US intelligence concerns about Alice Huang a year ago and did not take action. Nvidia has generated roughly 15 cents of every dollar the US stock market has returned since 2023. Jensen Huang has, meanwhile,
lobbied Trump
to ease restrictions on the sale of
advanced AI chips to China.
The US and China are battling for an edge in AI development. See inside the underground network to get

DoorDash Buys Instacart
Food and retail delivery app DoorDash
is acquiring
grocery-focused rival Instacart for $17B, the companies announced yesterday. DoorDash shares rose 5.6% on the news; Instacart shares slid 2.2%.
DoorDash handles nearly 61% of all restaurant deliveries, ahead of Uber Eats (26%). The platform already partners with 2,700 Kroger stores and 600 Costco warehouses in addition to several regional grocers. Instacart has partnerships across 1,800 chains to own roughly 21% of online grocery sales, trailing Amazon and Walmart’s collective 47% market share. The acquisition marks DoorDash’s latest effort to broaden courier offerings beyond restaurant deliveries. Through partnerships with Macy’s, Target, and other retailers, the company has enabled same-day deliveries of clothing, electronics, and more.
